claims.text: Every risk an organisation has is already accepted; somebody is carrying it today, and the only questions worth asking are who has accepted it and until when.
claims.quote: Every risk your organisation has is already accepted.

claims.text: A risk exists the moment the exposure does; nobody decides whether to accept it, and the organisation carries it from the start, signed for or not.
claims.quote: A risk exists the moment the exposure does.

claims.text: There is no deny button: as risks.sgit.ai puts it, you cannot vote a fact out of existence, and a register that lets you reject a risk lets you pretend.
claims.quote: You cannot vote a fact out of existence.

claims.text: The only real choices are three, accept it for a stated interval, fund the work that reduces it, or fix it; deferral is not a fourth door and an unaccepted risk is treated as critical and rolls up.
claims.quote: Deferral is not a fourth door.

claims.text: Every acceptance is for an interval, and the interval is the decision, because each length names a different response.
claims.quote: It is the decision, because each length names a different response.

claims.text: If the honest answer to how long we can live with this is four hours, the organisation is not managing a risk but responding to an incident.
claims.quote: If the honest answer to "how long can we live with this?" is four hours, the organisation is not managing a risk any more; it is responding to one.

value.unit: hours, the acceptance that is an incident

claims.text: One month, assemble and fund, is the default interval, set deliberately just above the incident line; six months is a legitimate decision to wait, with a name on it.
claims.quote: | 1 month | Assemble and fund. The default, set deliberately just above the incident line. |

claims.text: When the interval ends nothing silently continues: the same decision returns to the same desk, and if nobody acts the risk goes one level up.
claims.quote: When the interval ends, nothing silently continues.

claims.text: Accepted is an act by a named person on a date for an interval; acceptable is a threshold, the point at which the business is happy to stop funding remediation.
claims.quote: Accepted is an act: a named person, on a date, for an interval. Acceptable is a threshold

claims.text: Article 9(5) of the EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to leave residual risk judged to be acceptable, and the Act never defines acceptable.
claims.quote: The Act never defines "acceptable".

claims.text: Being over or under the acceptable line does not remove the need for somebody to accept what is carried; acceptance has to happen every time a risk exists.
claims.quote: Acceptance has to happen every time a risk exists. The only debate is for how long, and for what action.

claims.text: Every risk has a holder, every holder has a boss, so every risk has a chain and every chain ends at the board, computed rather than reported.
claims.quote: So every risk has a chain, and every chain ends at the board.

claims.text: In the Risk Graph Explorer's role risk map the CTO holds 4 risks and sees 25 pass through, and the board has 37 arrive.
claims.quote: The CTO holds 4 and sees 25 pass through; the board has 37 arrive.

claims.text: Nobody can accept on anybody else's behalf; a boss sees the risk arrive and whether it was accepted, and a refusal is visible as a finding rather than a failure.
claims.quote: nobody can accept on anybody else's behalf.

claims.text: A fractal risk register, as graphs.sgit.ai describes it: wherever there is a stakeholder accepting a risk, that entity needs a register.
claims.quote: wherever there is a stakeholder accepting a risk, that entity needs a register.

claims.text: A database administrator's risk translates into the CISO's, the CFO's, the CEO's and the board's, each in that person's words joined by named edges; the vocabulary changes at every altitude and the grammar does not.
claims.quote: The vocabulary changes at every altitude. The grammar does not

claims.text: The single change that closes the gap between a register and reality is that every risk names the facts that make it true and the facts that would end it.
claims.quote: every risk names the facts that make it true, and the facts that would end it.

claims.text: In the Risk Graph Explorer a risk is established by one cited fact and carries its own end condition, so it ships with its own falsification condition.
claims.quote: The risk ships with its own falsification condition.

claims.text: In the six-week replay the risk is established on day 0, accepted for two weeks, expires and escalates on day 15, materialises on day 24, and ceases on evidence on day 42.
claims.quote: and on day 42 it ceases, on evidence

value.unit: days from establishment to cessation in the replay

claims.text: On day 15 the two-week acceptance expired with its action undone, so the risk rolled up to the platform owner, who had to accept, fund or fix.
claims.quote: The two-week acceptance expired with its action undone, so the risk rolled up to the platform owner

claims.text: At the same moment the register row still says open until the committee in December with no evidence attached; that difference is the air gap.
claims.quote: That difference is the air gap.

claims.text: Every material risk deserves a vault of its own as the evidence pack of governance, holding its facts, controls, acceptances, escalations, incidents and the evidence that ended it.
claims.quote: Every material risk deserves a place to keep its own story

claims.text: A vault per material risk is a proposal, not yet a practice; the published method describes fractal registers and a chain to the board, and the vault idea is new here.
claims.quote: This is a proposal, not yet a practice

claims.text: On twins.sgit.ai every acceptance is performed by a twin acting for a person, and risks become testable, but the twins site says plainly that none of this is built.
claims.quote: None of this is built.

claims.text: Taking risk acceptance to market with RiskMandate from the angle of AI agents and insurability was hard for two reasons, ownership and resistance.
claims.quote: With RiskMandate.ai we approached risk acceptance from the angle of AI agents and insurability, and it was hard for two reasons.

claims.text: Executives resist, rationally, because accepting everything they hold changes their job; risks.sgit.ai says no-deny is the strongest idea and the hardest to sell, and names interval inflation as the way to defeat it.
claims.quote: No-deny is the strongest idea here and the hardest to sell.

claims.text: The model works in the gaps the GRC platforms leave, and the owner thinks the GRC vendors should sponsor and integrate with it rather than compete.
claims.quote: I think the GRC vendors should be sponsoring and integrating with this work rather than competing with it

claims.text: An engine that records acceptances, runs the clocks and fires at expiry does not exist yet; risks.sgit.ai states that essentially none of its model is implemented in code.
claims.quote: an engine that records acceptances, runs the clocks and fires at expiry

claims.text: The published material leaves open what happens at expiry, whether an unaccepted risk rolls up automatically or waits, and which of two published interval scales is canonical.
claims.quote: The published material also leaves open exactly what happens at expiry

claims.text: This should be a company, possibly several, and the Risk Acceptance Office vault holds the business plan: the operating model, services and prices as hypotheses, go-to-market starting from the resistance, and the first ninety days.
claims.quote: I think this should be a company, and possibly several.

claims.text: The pitch is two questions asked of any register: who has accepted this, and until when?
claims.quote: who has accepted this, and until when?
